author: Mariana Hernandez
title: Forty Billion. Not For You - by Mariana Hernandez
text:
You. Me. Us.
We keep hearing the same sermon:
We’re in debt. We’re out of money. We can’t afford your doctor, your groceries, your home.
Then—like a magic trick they don’t bother hiding—
Washington finds $40 billion for Argentina.
Read that again.
Twenty billion now, in a shiny currency swap.
Another twenty billion they’re trying to wrangle from bankers and funds.
Forty billion in headlines.
While your kid’s school sells candy so the library can buy books.
Make it make sense.
Property taxes—higher.
Rents—higher.
Foreclosures—rising.
Grocery bill—anxiety attack.
Eggs—sticker shock.
Gas—creeping up (again).
Insurance—don’t even start. Some families staring at near-doubling premiums next renewal.
You open your banking app like it’s a horror movie.
You stand at the pharmacy counter and do math with your pulse in your throat.
You skip the doctor until it’s an emergency because emergencies are the only thing we fund anymore.
And while you’re juggling overdue notices, the government is “shut down.”
Not because America ran out of money but because the people in charge are arguing over who deserves care.
They argue about who gets seen by a doctor, whose child gets medicine,
who is “too costly,” who is “someone else’s problem.”
They say we can’t afford health services for everyone.
They debate the billions spent on clinics and hospitals about $4 billion a year , according to public-health studies and call it waste.
But somehow there’s forty billion tax dollars ready to wire abroad to Argentina.
They dress it up nice— stabilizing markets , countering China , policy not politics.
Please.
This lands weeks before Argentina’s election.
It props up an economy led by a president who can’t tame inflation at home.
It buys leverage abroad while selling struggle here.
That’s not compassion.
That’s theater with a Treasury seal.
We’re not out of money.
We’re out of honesty.
Because when cancer trials close for “lack of funds,”
and food-stamp offices turn off the lights early,
and teachers buy their own supplies,
and nurses bring blankets from home,
and veterans wait months to be seen
the same people telling you there’s no money
find forty billion for a foreign bailout.
They love that word debt.
They polish it. They weaponize it.
Debt is the reason you can’t have insulin,
but not the reason a foreign government can have a lifeline.
Debt is the reason your clinic closes,
but not the reason a central bank across the equator gets dollar oxygen.
Debt is their excuse.
Priorities are their policy.
You already know this.
When America truly wants to pay for something, it pays.
War? Paid.
Bailouts? Paid.
Forty-billion “stabilization” packages timed to elections? Paid.
But your health?
Your food?
Your housing?
Priced out.
Not because we’re broke because we’re being spent in the wrong direction.
Help the world, sure. Be generous, sure.
But not while our own house is on fire and they’re selling our water by the gallon.
I’m not mad at Argentina.
I’m mad at a leadership class that will wire billions abroad
while telling a mother in Cleveland, a teacher in Fresno, a veteran in Tampa,
“Sorry. We’re tapped out.”
We’re not tapped out.
We’re just not the priority.
They say we’re broke.
They say we can’t afford you.
Then they send $40 billion to Argentina.
Call it aid if you need a bedtime story.
I call it a policy confession:
When the powerful want it, they find the money.
When you need it, they find a reason.
And I’m done pretending that’s anything but theft with paperwork.
